query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: When additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is exposed at elevated temperatures under oxidizing conditions, enhanced grain-boundary diffusion promotes the nucleation and coarsening of deleterious intergranular precipitates (e.g., Cr‐rich sigma phase and fine nitrides) that weaken grain-boundary cohesion, thereby predisposing the alloy to catastrophic failure under mechanical load. In contrast, samples aged under reducing conditions will exhibit fewer of these precipitates and retain higher grain-boundary integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐built, additively manufactured high-entropy alloy with a predominantly single-phase FCC matrix, minimal secondary phase precipitation, and intact grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to prolonged high-temperature heat treatments (e.g., within 950–1300 K) in atmospheres with either high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) or low oxygen/reducing conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature annealing for extended durations (e.g., 100–1000 hours) where diffusion-driven processes are active; experiments should compare atmospheres that differ markedly in their oxygen potential.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary regions where intergranular precipitates (such as Cr-rich sigma phase and nitrides) accumulate or where nonuniform, poorly adherent oxide scales form.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperatures increase atomic mobility and, in oxidizing environments, oxygen enhances grain-boundary diffusion. This promotes the nucleation and growth of brittle intergranular phases that disrupt the cohesive strength of the FCC matrix, leading to loss of ductility and catastrophic failure under stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built baseline and reducing environment samples, the oxidized samples will exhibit a higher volume fraction and coarser intergranular precipitates (or poorly adherent oxide layers), reduced fracture toughness, lower ductility, and an earlier onset of catastrophic failure when subjected to mechanical testing.
generation.baseline: The initially homogeneous FCC alloy with minimal secondary phase formation and intact grain-boundary cohesion prior to any high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant for prolonged exposures within the temperature range of approximately 950–1300 K (or equivalently around 700–1000 °C), where diffusion-driven precipitation or oxidation processes become active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics and relative contributions of precipitate formation versus oxidation-induced bonding changes may vary with slight differences in gas composition and temperature; further testing is needed to separate these effects under controlled conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identically additively manufactured alloy samples and subject them to high-temperature aging (e.g., at 1100 K for 500 hours) in two controlled atmospheres: one oxidizing (high oxygen partial pressure) and one reducing. Subsequently, use TEM/SEM (with EDS) to image and quantify intergranular precipitate (or oxide scale) formation at grain boundaries, and perform mechanical tests (tensile, microhardness, fracture toughness) to evaluate ductility and failure characteristics.
measurements: Grain-boundary precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution (or oxide scale quality)
Mechanical properties including fracture toughness, ductility, and microhardness
Comparison of failure modes between samples exposed to oxidizing and reducing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples aged under oxidizing conditions do not show a statistically significant increase in intergranular precipitates (or formation of a nonuniform oxide scale) along with corresponding degradation of mechanical properties relative to reducing conditions, then the hypothesis that such grain-boundary degradation governs catastrophic failure is falsified.

In both cases it is important to control the new phase precipitation or dissolution upon heat treatment. The effect of non-equilibrium processing of SLM is also a great amount of residual stresses, a dense dislocation network, impurities and fine precipitation phases at boundaries []. This defective state was considered in this work as responsible for both the mechanical properties and microstructure evolution during high-temperature aging. Specifically, we reported on the tetragonal σ phase formation in FCC CoCrFeMnNi after thermomechanical processing comprising a room temperature thickness reduction of 90% and subsequent prolonged annealing. Prolonged annealing times were used because of the sluggish diffusion effect that slows down phase transformation. In addition, cold working was used to accelerate phase precipitation [,].

Whereas up to a certain working temperature fine precipitates can play a reinforcing role, starting from a temperature of about 950 K, the σ phase tends to swell and to preferentially place itself on the grain boundaries of the alloy. This in turn can lead to a significant reduction of the mechanical and chemical properties. This is described in the following and confirmed by a mechanical characterization with microhardness and hardness measurements that correlate with the microstructural evolution that occurs during aging.
Correlating with the microstructural and XRD investigations, these mechanical tests can provide important information on the stability and metastability of these high entropy alloys.

Unlike the classical Cantor alloys obtained by casting technology, the alloy obtained by SLM did not require prolonged exposure to high temperatures to produce secondary phase precipitation. SLM technology with Nitrogen protective atmosphere induced a fine secondary phases precipitation of nitrides and intermetallic phases in the as-built state. The cold-rolled plus annealed FCC matrix became unstable and secondary phases precipitated. The observed precipitation was made of tetragonal Cr-rich σ phase and of mixed Cr-(Fe, Mn, Co, Ni)-nitrides which nucleated at the triple points. The size of the σ phase precipitates increased with annealing temperature. When the annealing temperature was below the recrystallization temperature, the size of precipitates was small due to a low diffusion rate and confined at the grain boundaries of the as-built dendritic structure. When the temperature exceeded 1323 K, the σ phase dissolved and the alloy substantially returned to single phase with near equiatomic composition. σ phase and nitride precipitations yielded a significant alloy hardening only at room temperature and for annealing up to 923 K, that is, below recrystallization temperature. drafts.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy, degradation at elevated temperatures is primarily driven by selective elemental oxidation and interfacial segregation—specifically, the preferential oxidation of Ti (and possibly its interaction with Cr and Al) at internal grain boundaries. This leads to the formation of a discontinuous, non-protective Ti-rich oxide layer that creates localized stress concentrations and promotes intergranular embrittlement. Under oxidizing conditions, such oxide scale formation accelerates degradation, while under reducing conditions, the absence of a continuous protective scale permits deleterious diffusion processes and phase destabilization that similarly prime the alloy for catastrophic failure.
drafts.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a largely single-phase fcc matrix, minimal initial oxide scale, and relatively homogeneous elemental distribution tempered by typical AM microstructural features.
drafts.intervention: Expose samples to a systematically varied gas environment by independently adjusting the oxygen partial pressure in the test atmosphere. For instance, compare exposures in a high-oxygen (oxidizing) atmosphere versus a low-oxygen or mildly reducing atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperatures relevant to service conditions (e.g., 700–900 °C) under controlled gas compositions with defined oxygen partial pressures; exposure times sufficient to allow oxide scale evolution and microstructural changes (e.g., tens to hundreds of hours).
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions where selective oxidation leads to Ti-enriched oxide formation, and possibly associated with the formation of discontinuous oxide phases that weaken intergranular cohesion.
drafts.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, Ti (with some influence of Cr and Al) oxidizes preferentially at grain boundaries forming a less adherent, non-protective oxide scale. Internal stresses induced by the growth of this oxide and its mismatch with the metallic matrix lead to crack initiation and propagation. Under reducing conditions, the absence of a robust protective oxide scale allows uncontrolled elemental diffusion and phase destabilization, which similarly compromises grain boundary integrity and leads to brittle failure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: In high oxygen partial pressure environments, one would observe the formation of discontinuous, Ti-rich oxide deposits localized at grain boundaries along with evidence of intergranular cracking. In reducing environments, there would be less pronounced oxide scale formation but increased signs of grain boundary diffusion, phase transformation, and embrittlement. In both cases, the initial performance baseline (with minimal oxidation and intact grain boundaries) would be significantly degraded, pushing the material towards catastrophic failure upon mechanical loading.
drafts.baseline: The as-fabricated high-entropy alloy in its fcc state prior to elevated-temperature exposure, showing a homogeneous microstructure with minimal oxide contamination and good grain boundary integrity.
drafts.boundary: Findings are expected to be valid for exposures at temperatures around 700–900 °C and gas environments with oxygen partial pressures that are either clearly oxidizing (well above equilibrium levels) or mildly reducing (below equilibrium, possibly with controlled additions of a reducing gas such as H2 or CO). Behavior beyond these temperature or gas composition extremes might involve additional mechanisms not covered in this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple identical samples of the alloy and expose them to a matrix of controlled gas environments: one set in a high oxygen partial pressure atmosphere and another in a low-oxygen (or mildly reducing) atmosphere while keeping temperature (700–900 °C) and exposure time constant. Carry out detailed microstructural and mechanical evaluations (using techniques such as electron microscopy, EDS mapping, and fracture toughness testing) before and after exposure.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of oxide scale thickness and composition at grain boundaries via TEM/EDS.
Microstructural characterization of grain boundary embrittlement (e.g., intergranular crack density) using SEM.
Mechanical property assessment through tensile or fracture tests to detect catastrophic failure modes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If differential exposure to high and low oxygen partial pressures does not result in statistically significant differences in the formation of Ti-rich, discontinuous oxide scales at grain boundaries (or corresponding differences in intergranular embrittlement and mechanical degradation), then the hypothesis that selective grain boundary oxidation governs the degradation mechanism would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The high-entropy alloy degrades at elevated temperatures because its initially homogeneous fcc matrix develops a nonuniform, weakly adherent oxide scale through selective oxidation of Al (and likely Cr) under oxidizing conditions and, conversely, undergoes internal oxidation and incipient phase destabilization under reducing conditions. These processes lead to stress accumulation and local embrittlement that ultimately result in catastrophic failure when oxide spallation or internal void coalescence undermines the load-bearing matrix.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, featuring a fine-grained, homogeneous fcc phase with minimal initial oxide coverage.
drafts.intervention: Change the gas environment in a controlled manner: expose samples to oxidizing conditions (pure O2 or O2 with controlled H2O vapor) as well as to reducing conditions (H2-rich mixture), all at elevated temperatures.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperatures in the range of 800°C to 1000°C for extended periods, with carefully regulated gas compositions and humidity levels.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation, uniformity, and adhesion quality of the surface oxide scale (primarily Al-oxide and Cr-oxide), and the possible onset of internal oxidation or phase segregation beneath the scale.
drafts.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the preferential oxidation of aluminum (and possibly chromium) leads to the formation of a protective but nonuniform oxide scale. Thermal stresses during exposure eventually cause scale spallation and consequent oxygen penetration, which accelerates degradation and embrittlement. In reducing environments, suboptimal oxide scale formation allows oxygen ingress and internal oxidation, fostering elemental segregation and void formation that compromise structural integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-built baseline, specimens in oxidizing atmospheres will show thickening but increasingly defective oxide scales; spallation events should correlate with a rapid drop in mechanical strength. In reducing atmospheres, incomplete scale formation will lead to internal oxidation and microstructural changes (e.g., void formation or segregation) that gradually weaken the alloy. Furthermore, deliberate additions of water vapor in oxidizing conditions are expected to further accelerate scale rupture and the onset of catastrophic failure.
drafts.baseline: The as-built alloy, with a homogeneous microstructure and negligible oxide formation, exhibiting standard mechanical properties.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to exposures at 800°C–1000°C under gas atmospheres ranging from fully oxidizing (pure O2 or O2 with controlled humidity) to reducing (H2-rich mixtures).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of alloy samples and expose each set to one of three controlled atmospheres (pure oxidizing, oxidizing with added water vapor, and reducing) at 900°C for multiple durations. Following exposure, assess the surface oxide scale (via SEM/EDS for thickness, composition, and adhesion) and evaluate the internal microstructure (via cross-sectional microscopy for voids and phase changes). Mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and fatigue simulations) should correlate microstructural changes with degradation in performance.
measurements: presence and extent of internal oxidation or voids
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled atmospheric changes do not yield statistically significant variations in oxide scale morphology or degradation behavior (i.e., similar oxide characteristics and mechanical property degradation across all conditions), or if the onset and nature of catastrophic failure do not correlate with the predicted mechanisms (spallation under oxidizing conditions and internal oxidation under reducing conditions), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, exposure of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA to oxidizing (or reducing) gas environments accelerates intergranular diffusion that promotes the nucleation and growth of brittle, Cr-rich sigma‐phase and/or nitride precipitates at grain boundaries. These precipitates compromise grain cohesion and lower the ductility of the fine FCC matrix, predisposing the material to catastrophic failure under mechanical stress.
drafts.material_initial_state: The as-built alloy exhibits a homogeneous, single-phase FCC structure with a fine microstructure and only minimal, dispersed secondary phases.
drafts.intervention: Expose samples to controlled elevated-temperature aging (T ≥ 950 K) while systematically varying the gas atmosphere between oxidizing (high oxygen partial pressure) and reducing conditions.
drafts.conditions: Long-term thermal exposure (e.g., 100–1000 hours) at temperatures at or above ~950 K in environments that simulate either oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and coarsening of Cr-rich sigma-phase and/or nitride precipitates preferentially along grain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility, and in an oxidizing gas the enhanced surface oxidation (or in a reducing gas the lack of stabilizing oxides) alters the local chemistry. This drives preferential diffusion of Cr and possibly Ti to grain boundary regions where they form brittle intermetallic (sigma) or nitride phases. The growth of these intergranular precipitates deteriorates cohesion between grains, leading to early crack initiation and catastrophic failure under load.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built baseline, samples aged at or above 950 K in an oxidizing atmosphere will exhibit increased size and volume fraction of intergranular precipitates, reduced ductility, and a lower critical stress for intergranular fracture. In a reducing atmosphere, the absence of a stable protective oxide may also lead to surface degradation and embrittlement, albeit via potentially different kinetics. Mechanical tests (e.g., microhardness and tensile) should reveal a marked drop in ductility and increased brittleness correlating with the precipitate evolution.
drafts.baseline: The initial, homogenous FCC phase with low precipitate content and intact intergranular cohesion observed immediately after additive manufacturing.
drafts.boundary: This degradation mechanism is expected to dominate for prolonged exposures (hundreds of hours) at temperatures above approximately 950 K, when diffusion-controlled precipitate coarsening becomes significant.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and subject them to identical thermal exposures (e.g., 1000 K for 500 hours) under carefully controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. Characterize the microstructure before and after exposure using high-resolution SEM/EDS and XRD to quantify precipitate formation (size, distribution, and volume fraction) at grain boundaries. Simultaneously, perform mechanical testing (microhardness, tensile ductility) to correlate microstructural evolution with mechanical performance.
measurements: Precipitate size and volume fraction via SEM/EDS
Microhardness values and tensile ductility (e.g., reduction in strain-to-failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant increase in intergranular precipitates (or change in their morphology/distribution) is observed after exposure under either gas atmosphere, or if mechanical tests do not indicate reduced ductility or grain-boundary failure compared to the as-built baseline, then the hypothesis that precipitate-induced intergranular embrittlement governs degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, exposure to oxidizing gas accelerates grain-boundary diffusion and nucleation of Cr-rich sigma phase and fine nitride precipitates in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA. This intergranular precipitation rapidly embrittles the FCC matrix, making it prone to catastrophic failure via grain-boundary decohesion.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a mostly single-phase FCC structure that contains residual stresses, a dense dislocation network, and only minimal or very fine secondary precipitates.
drafts.intervention: Heat treatment at elevated temperatures (approximately 950–1300 K) for extended durations under controlled gas atmospheres: one group under oxidizing (oxygen-rich) conditions and a comparison group under reducing conditions.
drafts.conditions: Exposure temperatures between 950 K and 1300 K with long-term annealing (e.g., 100–1000 hours) in atmospheres that differ substantially in oxygen potential, ensuring that diffusion-driven secondary phase formation is thermally activated.
drafts.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary accumulation and growth of Cr-rich sigma phase and nitride precipitates.
drafts.mechanism: In oxidizing environments, increased oxygen availability enhances atomic mobility at grain boundaries and surfaces, promoting the nucleation and coarsening of brittle sigma phase and nitride precipitates. These precipitates disrupt grain boundary cohesion and reduce the alloy’s overall ductility, thereby triggering intergranular fracture and catastrophic failure under mechanical loads.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared with samples exposed under reducing conditions, those treated in oxidizing atmospheres will display a significantly higher volume fraction and coarser grain-boundary precipitates. This will correlate with reduced fracture toughness, lower ductility, and an earlier onset of catastrophic failure when mechanically stressed.
drafts.baseline: The original additive-manufactured HEA with a homogeneous FCC matrix, minimal secondary phase precipitation, and good ductility and strength.
drafts.boundary: Temperature range from about 950 K to 1300 K and long exposure durations (hundreds of hours) where diffusion-driven precipitation becomes significant; effects are specifically expected under high oxygen potential (oxidizing gases) compared to low oxygen potential (reducing gases).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples. Divide them into two groups for annealing at a target elevated temperature (e.g., 1100 K) for a fixed duration (e.g., 500 hours) in two atmospheres: an oxygen-rich (oxidizing) environment and a reducing atmosphere with minimal oxygen. After exposure, characterize the microstructure (using TEM/SEM with EDS) to assess the presence, fraction, and size of grain-boundary sigma phase and nitride precipitates. Conduct mechanical testing (e.g., microhardness, tensile, and fracture toughness tests) to correlate changes in mechanical performance with microstructure.
measurements: Volume fraction and size distribution of grain-boundary precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing environment does not yield a statistically significant increase in grain-boundary precipitate formation and corresponding degradation in mechanical properties (relative to samples annealed in reducing conditions) or if catastrophic failure does not correlate with the formation of these precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.
